utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After that dramatic opening, Your Honour, it's Joanna Korner together with Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So today, on the other side, we can see two counsel, happy enough. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I take the opportunity today once again to ask Dr. Stakic about the health condition. Are there any problems in the Detention Unit you wanted to address?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Currently, I do not have any health problems, nor are there any significant problems that I would like to raise in respect of the Detention Unit, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to recall in the presence of both Defence counsel that as it was indicated in the beginning of the case, it will be, and it's, of course, still your right whenever you want to make a statement in the framework of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This means that when you believe it is necessary and after having discussed this issue together with your Defence counsel to appear as a witness probably only related to the one or other issue. Maybe the question what was the reason from your point of view why you did not continue as it apparently seems to be after that what we have heard from Witness Beglerbegovic. And in addition, as mentioned before, from the point of view of the Judges, it is also your right to give, under the rules, a statement, if you so want and after having discussed this with your Defence counsel. I only wanted to recall this when we discussed last week this question of the finalisation of this part addressed in the indictment before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for having sat down. I thought you had finished, Your Honour. But I have taken note of your explanation. I understand it. And I should like to thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, any administrative matters? What about the witness for -- you may be seated, please. What about the witness? Is the problem resolved for next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it is, Your Honour. I think the witness will be here, as I understand it. Mr. Koumjian was dealing with it, and will be coming into court later to deal with the other matter I raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The last message I heard one hour ago from the Registrar in person, he told me that he will do the -- that it will be possible to hear this witness. And as it was said already yesterday, the Defence was prepared to continue this way. Then we would have two additional witnesses for next week, for the beginning of the week. And what about today after --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, there's no witness after Mr. Mayhew because we worked roughly on the basis that he would take two full sessions. I think, in fact, again we slightly overestimated, but I don't know how much Mr. Ostojic has for Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good. So nothing else is foreseen for today that we can draw the conclusion that afterwards, we can conclude today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we thought -- we do have some more documents, a list which may require reading. But I know that there are a couple of administrative matters, or at least one, to deal with this question of the documents we received yesterday from the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You see me as a big question mark. Which documents are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The documents that Your Honour referred to in the order. We have been supplied with a photocopy of what was clearly an original and we want to raise that. We need original documents to do the testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt. Anything from your side to be addressed before the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the witness may be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated immediately. And same applies as was said yesterday; you are still under the solemn declaration from yesterday when now listening to the questions of the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mayhew, my name is John Ostojic and along with Mr. Branko Lukic I represent Dr. Stakic. I'm going to ask you a few questions in connection with your testimony yesterday which I've had the opportunity to review, as well as your reports that were provided to the OTP. Yesterday I noticed, reading the transcript, that at times because we both speak English, that you and the OTP did overlap and there was an issue, so to the extent that I pause, it's only to give an opportunity for everyone to get the proper and complete translation and give you an opportunity to reflect on the question and provide us with a complete answer. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I notice in the witness statement that you provided to the OTP on March 14th and 15th, 2000, you state as your current occupation being that of a consultant. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly what you currently do?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm self-employed, and I work as an advisor to aid agencies and a trainer of aid workers. And I also work for the government if they need advice on policy. I also lecture a certain amount, particularly at the British Military Staff College and other military and the European Police College on humanitarian agencies and how they work in order to explain the realities on the ground, in a situation such as a peacekeeping operation with a humanitarian operation happening beside.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In particular, can you share with us which aid agencies you are consulting with currently?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Currently, only one group of aid agencies, which is known as the Emergency Personnel Network. It includes quite a number of aid agencies, but prominent among them are the British Red Cross, Save the Children Fund UK, an organisation called Redar, Engineers for Disaster Relief, and a number of others. That's the only client I have at the present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Since 1992 to the present, have you ever worked for any agency affiliated with the ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been an evaluator on a mission of a number of weeks for a group of aid agencies called Action by Churches Together. This is the humanitarian arm of the World Council of Churches. And because of that, it does include churches based in the Balkan region including, for example, the Orthodox church. So to that extent, yes, I have had connection with aid operations in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any others other than that which you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: None come to mind at present, but I could check if that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may ask you a general question with respect to your preparation for the work that you did commencing March of 1992 in Zagreb and in Bosnia, were you familiar with the various conferences and meetings that were taking place throughout Europe during that timeframe? Specifically, I'm referencing the London Conference, the Lisbon meetings, as well as the Geneva agreement of May 22, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I don't recall the Lisbon or Geneva meetings. I do recall the London Conference. The general answer to the question is yes, I would be aware of all major meetings of that kind. However, my work was usually at the ground level and not concerned with the high-level diplomacy as I but only in so far as it, more or less, directly affected my work at ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to state that you were doing on the ground was an attempt to influence what was happening at the higher diplomatic level?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times, there will be a direct connection. If we verified an event on the ground, that would have an impact, of course, elsewhere. Our overall aim was to prevent fighting and to persuade people not to fight. But -- and so our actions on the ground would be directed to that end. But we would only, I think, seek to influence negotiations at a higher level by the use of verified fact on the ground if we felt that facts on the ground were not being taken into account properly or fully at these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that you were there to verify certain facts, who would give you an assignment as to which facts you should verify? Were you just given one task and say, if you look and examine this issue and have the seven people such as yourself along with the three or four interpreters that I think accompanied you, who would give you the task and can you tell us what was the game plan for verification of those facts or rumours as you've identified them yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, we were not given specific tasks for our daily work. We were given an overall aim to follow, which was to report in a balanced and accurate way on the situation on the ground, specifically to make sure that we were including all viewpoints and speaking to a balanced mix of interlocutors. So we were a monitor mission. It was to report a general understanding of the whole picture, as far as we could obtain it. Within that, we were not frequently, I think probably very rarely, given specific verification tasks. However, that did happen at times, and in particular, I recall in Croatia before I moved to Bosnia being sent to a number of villages to verify the situation in those specific villages where certain allegations of ethnic cleansing by Croats against Serbs had been alleged. And they wanted facts and figures to be put on to those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that was at one time also the area of Derventa, correct, that you actually verified certain facts?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't recall at the moment being asked to verify a particular detail in Derventa but it was possible we were asked to do so. Our primary work there was in the context of our normal aim of reporting on the whole situation, doing what we could to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if you were ever given a task in March or April of 1992 to investigate a massacre of Serbs in the area called Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain of that name. It would be easy to check that with the reports. If there was a task given, it would have been reported on by me and it would be in the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The reports that were introduced as evidence yesterday that you reviewed, would it be fair to say that that is a complete and comprehensive litany of the reports that you provided to your superiors during your stay from March all the way through September of 1992, and obviously excepting that there was an intermittent period in which you were not present in the area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not complete. There are a number of reports not present in what we talked about yesterday. I would normally provide a daily report when out on the ground, or possibly my teammate would do it. Typically, it would be me because of my native English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was your teammate at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about March and April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varied. In Derventa, it was a man called Botonakis, a Greek colonel, and I probably teamed up with other members of the team. We formed teams usually of two monitors plus a driver plus an interpreter, and that tended to mix around depending on people's leave periods and the needs of the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a situation involving again in the period of March, April 1992 of a massacre in Kupres?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that specific massacre. You must understand that there were many massacres, and certainly many more allegations of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. massacres. And strange though it may seem now, unless I was engaged particularly on a task concerning that, the many allegations became -- I didn't pay particular attention to remembering every single allegation because there were so many, and the situation was confused, fast-changing, and we had to be quite ruthless in our prioritisation of what was our primary task that day when there was so much else that we could be trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us once you left Zagreb and came to Bosnia and in the Prijedor area, if you know geographically how far Prijedor is from the Croatian border at that time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if it was approximately 30 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here, do you have a different estimate that it may be far more or far less than 30 kilometres from the Croatian border is where Prijedor is situated?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's a fair question after ten years. I'm very experienced with maps and geography. At the time, I would have had a very accurate idea of the layout. I have a feeling that it could be that sort of distance or greater, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion, sir, if it's established that indeed there were massacres that were occurring by Croatians and/or Muslims of the Serbian civilians and population in March and April of 1992, what effect would it have on the Serbian population in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would make them very afraid and very angry. It would lead some to want to take action, and it would lead some to take action, and we frequently came across reports on all three sides of military, paramilitary, and apparently civilian people taking extra-judicial, violent action against people of the other group. It was certainly not constricted -- restricted to one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, if you recall ever verifying that there was a massacre of Serbs in any part of Croatia or Bosnia in March and April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only would have verified any event in an area to which I was deployed. I was deployed briefly in Croatia before I went to Bosnia, and I did not go to verify a massacre of Serbs in that time. I had fairly brief missions. I did, however, verify ethnic expulsions, commonly known as ethnic cleansing of Serbs by Croats, and that was my first experience of that phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, whether or not there was a Croatian/Muslim coalition that was acting in concert together against the Serbs at any time during your stay at that former territory, either Croatia or in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say "certainly," how did you come to learn that there was a coalition between Croatians and Muslims against the Serbs in Bosnia, during the period of time of March through September 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was widely reported by our teams and by others that in central and southwest Bosnia there was a Muslim/Croat coalition. That's one point, and I think that's a matter of widely known historical record. I wasn't personally in that area, but I was dealing with reports from there. As for northern Bosnia, my time in Derventa, for example, the town divided into an area controlled by a Muslim and Croat coalition, and an area controlled by the Bosnian Serb groupings. I will just urge a little caution on the record "coalition," that it could be subject to a various -- varying interpretations. But it was certainly the Muslims and Croats working together in Derventa at that time. And the nature of the coalition might have been quite fleeting, temporary, and insubstantial, or might have been much more permanent, and we weren't aware of the precise nature of that coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me what --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Could I ask what the relevance of these questions is about Derventa and areas outside Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would the Court like me to reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, the witness obviously testified to that in his direct examination yesterday. It's also included in his report. The other most important issue is the Court knows Manjaca is a military camp that is not subject to the indictment against the accused. Yet, there were numerous questions asked by the Prosecutor and testimony elicited by this witness, and I think to put the witness in the proper perspective and to get the complete picture, as he himself states in his testimony and in his report, it's necessary for the Court to understand, we believe, and it's relevant to understand the entire climate as opposed to take the events leading up to Prijedor in a vacuum so that they may ultimately be fully -- more fully understood by all. So we think the time and the scope of it is enormously close, and would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I do not disagree. The only point is, indeed, the witness appears, at least for me, more or less an opinion witness. But I think we can raise any objections balancing objections in the two directions. And we didn't interrupt the OTP when discussing the issue -- this issue, and indeed, it may be fact-based, fact-based important to hear something more about the background and the development leading to this what forms --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly think it's relevant. One, I deliberately did not ask questions about Manjaca, except to put in to context Trnopolje. I omitted all the reports and everything that dealt with Manjaca. So to say that I asked questions about Manjaca is not correct. But secondly, Your Honour, I am not aware that I asked any questions about anything outside the area of Prijedor. But if Your Honour thinks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you feel like being criticised, it's a totally wrong approach. I just want to recall that we discussed in depth the report of the CSCE mission to inspect places of detention in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and there it is indeed important, and you stressed indeed this point, the overview - I don't know the name - the places of detentions, it was annex E leading, and I think it's correct, not only to Manjaca and Trnopolje, but giving us the overview of places of detention open until this point in time. And the context is important, as it was already pointed out by the OTP in the entire beginning of this case when discussing these issues on the basis of Dr. Donia's report. Therefore, I think it's only fair to hear -- to grant the Defence the possibility to ask these questions covered already earlier by Mr. Donia, and it was -- my remark was not related at all to that what you asked yesterday, save these parts where indeed reference was made also to other parts of former Yugoslavia, in this case Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, just a couple more questions if I may, and I know you hesitate to use the word "Croatian and Muslim coalition," respecting that, what would you call it, then? A partnership or a coexistence or how would you like me to call it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not hesitate to use the word "coalition". I simply want it to be clear that it is subject to various interpretations. And when I use the world "coalition" I am not making a statement about exactly what kind of relationship it was. I'm sorry, I'm getting all tangled up here. Because I don't think we were aware of the precise nature of that relationship, as indeed we were not aware of the internal goings on at that higher level, generally in all the three communities. So I'm quite happy with the world "coalition." I just put in a caveat about its precise meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll accept your interpretation for the moment of that and we will work with that. How early if you know, was this coalition between the Croatian and Muslim groups formed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think it's important to know with respect to the events that took place in April through August of 1992 to have verified whether or not the coalition between the Croatians and Muslims occurred before April of 1992 or after September of 1992? That would be relevant. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relevant to political judgements. I was not in the business of making major political judgements. We would report the facts that we found, and when we discovered that there was such a relationship, we would report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But was the coalition only, sir, as far as you knew that which existed in March of 1992? I mean, that's when you first learned or understood that there was a coalition between the two Croatian and Muslim groups. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when I first learned that. But it would have been in March or April 1992, but bear in mind I arrived in the region in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was the coalition, sir, to the best of your knowledge and opinion, a coalition only on a political level or was it also a coalition of a military kind as well?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Derventa, it was -- it seemed to us to be of a military or paramilitary kind as well, in the sense that men had taken up arms, both Muslim and Croat men, within Derventa and were facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if the Croatian authorities, military, were ever providing Muslims with arms to fight against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never able to verify arms' supplies by anyone, as far as I recall, within the ECMM. We had a strong suspicion that Croatia was supplying arms at least to the Bosnian Croat forces, regular or irregular. And since the Muslims and Croats were cooperating in Derventa at least and elsewhere as we've already mentioned, we suspected that arms might be reaching the Muslim side as well from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For clarification, Exhibit S217 was provisionally marked, it's the report of the CSCE mission to inspect places of detention in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 29 August through 4th September, 1992. Sir, is this the report that was filed by Sir John Thomson?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's the basis of some of the opinions that you're providing to the Court and your testimony yesterday, it was this specific exhibit that you reviewed or this report, as well as the report by Mr. Charles McLeod. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That report is not the basis of my opinions. That would not be correct. However, I was asked yesterday whether I agreed with a number of parts of it and to the report in general, and my answers were to that group of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when you were asked that yesterday in open session or at any time prior to reviewing this report, did you find anything you disagreed with in the report?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in general, I agreed with -- I agreed with it. It's possible that there are small parts which I disagreed with, but they don't come to mind. In general, I thought it was a fair report and well Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. written.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, with respect to this report, specifically annex D --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I may have the Court have the Registrar provide a copy of that to him so Mr. Mayhew may have it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. The pages that I have are not completely numbered, so if you just look at the top, you'll be able to find the annex D that I refer to. It appears on ER number 00999598.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This was part of the report when you reviewed the report, correct, and it's, in essence, an agreement which was an invitation of the International Red Cross between the three ethnic parties in Bosnia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact I haven't read this annex. I didn't read the whole report but only those aspects that seemed to me directly relevant to my area of work with the team, particularly what we saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I feel it as my obligation to caution the witness. You were asked beforehand whether or not you agree with the entire, to a certain extent, with the entire report. And at that time already, you should have told the Court that you haven't read the entire report. Otherwise, it could be the wrong testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. By way of explanation, I have taken -- This annex is an attached agreement, and I took the question to mean the report as written by the authors. Perhaps that was a loose term of language, but this is an agreement outside the scope of the mission's work and outside the scope of the work on the ground. And I apologise if I appeared to mislead. There was no intention to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You understood the admonition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you could turn to the second page of the report, and maybe we could, in a nutshell -- actually of the report not of the annex, Mr. Mayhew, second page of the report itself, which is 00999571, it starts with the word "Contents"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at least looking at the contents of this, what I thought was the report, which part did you read and which part did you not, and we'll get back to annex in a moment?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read parts 1, 2, and 3 which are the substantive parts of the report. The attached documents it seemed to me, were not in the main body of the report. I have, however, read the list of mission members, annex G; the notes on detention places visited by the mission, annex F; list of detention places visited by the mission, annex E; annex C, the memorandum on Trnopolje; annex B, the list of alleged detention places; and I looked at the map. So, in fact, annex D is the only annex I didn't read, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's just take a look at annex D. I have a couple questions with respect to that if I may. It states there was a meeting that took place in Geneva on the 22nd of May 1992 where discussions on different aspects of the application and implementation of international humanitarian law was discussed. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's right at the centre of the page on the first page of annex D.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that, sir, help refresh your recollection as to whether or not there was a meeting in Geneva on May 22nd, 1992 to discuss the different aspects, with respect to international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. I don't recall the meeting. There were, of course, many meetings at that time. So that is no surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Going down a couple paragraphs, it says also "Taking into consideration The Hague statement of the 5th November, 1991," are you familiar sir at all that there were meetings at The Hague here in the Netherlands involving the United Nations on or about November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim to have any specific memory of that meeting or of, no doubt, many other meetings at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there any reason we should doubt this annex and this report by Sir John Thomson which seems to indicate that there was a meeting at The Hague on or about November 5th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: None as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when you were preparing to go on the field in March of 1992, were you, sir, briefed with respect to the background of the different ethnic groups as well as the political proposed settlement that was taking place both at The Hague, in Geneva, as well as during the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had general briefings. They were not comprehensive, but they did include the background on the ethnic groups. They did include a summary of political events in recent times. But they were certainly not comprehensive, and we took steps to improve that in the course of the next few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand your testimony. Are you telling me that initially in March and April 1992 when you were on the Croatian front line if I can call it that, you weren't well informed, and then subsequent when you returned in August of 1992 you were given another briefing and you were more informed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not telling you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that briefings were not very full. There were briefings. We felt that they could be improved. When I returned to the headquarters later, one of my responsibilities at various times was to contribute to the initial briefing of newly arrived monitors, and we improved and lengthened the amount of briefing given to monitors later that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Having gone back to the area or the region of Bosnia in August of 1992, were you informed at any time, sir, whether or not this agreement was actually signed and agreed by all three parties, as reflected on annex D?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the agreement, and therefore, I can't comment on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if you were ever briefed or discussions were held in connection with provocation by various ethnic groups in trying to interfere and to actually derail the agreement that was being offered and that was being discussed at a higher diplomatic level during May 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many acts of provocation and attempts to derail political agreements on all sides. And that would no doubt have applied to this agreement, though I can't comment on the agreement in detail for the reason that I've given. But I was certainly aware, we all were, of that sort of provocation and contrary behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who informed you of those provocations?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a almost daily occurrence around the missionary, so by reading our reports, we would be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you sir at any time attempt to verify if, on May 22nd, there was a provocation by the Muslims against the Serbs in Hambarine, which is in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would that have been a significant item that if you had actually done any -- I want to call it an investigating, but any verification of that issue, that would have been something that you would have recorded. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but please correct me if I am wrong, the record will show the dates, but I think we had evacuated from northern Bosnia before the 22nd of May. We had no means of verifying anything in northern Bosnia on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But isn't it true, though, your job even in August was to verify what had transpired, to try to ease the tensions of the people, to bring the ethnic groups together, and in fact if there was a claim by the Serbs if there was a provocation on a checkpoint where a Serbian police officer was killed, allegedly, wasn't it part and parcel your job, sir, and only jour job of your mission to verify the truth of that allegation?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our job to verify everything we could in areas where we had the possibility. Where we were not able to go directly, we were, of course, not able to verify. We would often pass on reports that we had received, which were unverified by their very nature. They might be press reports or claims from one of the three sides. And it's quite possible that we passed on reports on that. But since we were not able to go to the area, it would have been irresponsible for us to pronounce a judgement on what had or had not happened. And this goes to the very heart of the problem that we had in our mission, that where access was denied us or for other reasons we were not able to go to an area, typically security reasons, verification was impossible. And to claim to have verified would have been irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you left the area in May of 1992. And that was as a result of a death of one of your colleagues, correct, that occurred in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a major contributing reason, but there were other reasons. It was an overall assessment of the security situation throughout Bosnia. That event was the trigger for the decision which was taken soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to that unfortunate incident, can you give us a timeframe as to when it occurred? Was it before or after the alleged implementation of this agreement which was to take effect on the 26th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been before the 26th of May because we evacuated before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did your mission, sir, at any time investigate the perpetrators of that murder of your colleague in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact I was a part of the team of inquiry into that killing and murder correctly described. And as a result, I travelled to the area where it happened as soon as it became safe to do so. There was a delay because he was killed in no man's land, and it was not safe to go immediately. We did not investigate the perpetrators, although we tried to, because we concluded they were members of the Serb forces in that area. And we -- I mean, we ourselves had no power to investigate members of armed forces in a legal sense, and as I recall, when we passed our report on, action was not possible because of the Serb authorities' responses and refusal to allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What was the basis for your conclusion that it was the Serb forces who perpetrated this crime, not having your report here, not being able to evaluate what it is that you said in that report, but taking into consideration that you yourself stated that you could not and did not investigate that allegation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We do actually have -- I'm sorry. We have the report, if you want it. It has absolutely no relevance at all to this case, but we have the full report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I see it as an objection as to the relevance --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, I'm merely stating -- because I heard Mr. Ostojic assert this fact, so I thought I better let him know straight away if he thinks it's of relevance he can have the report. But I can't see the relevance at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, it's my understanding under the rules that they are required to provide us with his statements, his full report, although we appreciate their assistance that they have provided us on numerous occasions, the Defence does not wish for the OTP to determine for the Defence what is or is not relevant. The OTP, as it has with other witnesses, has provided us enormous amount of documents, without identifying whether they are relevant or under specifically Rule 68 or merely just provided it to us. We find it somewhat ironic, at least I do, Your Honour, respectfully, that here is a person who was involved in an incident that occurred on or about the timeframe which is within the period of the fourth amended revised indictment and she or the OTP makes a decision whether it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been making this decision all along. It couldn't have remotely occurred to anyone, and indeed, I will object to the relevance of this, that the investigation of a shooting of a monitor way out of the area that this case is concerned with, could be of the slightest relevance in any way, shape, or form to Dr. Stakic's case. And the complaint has been from -- in most cases that we load the Defence with documents that they don't need. But, Your Honour, I'm merely pointing out to Mr. Os Stojic and I'm now going to ask Mr. Ostojic to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. justify why it is relevant for this Court to hear about the report of a shooting of an ECMM monitor completely unconnected with the events in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I'd like to address and answer that specific question, but I'd like to do so outside the presence of Mr. Mayhew if I may, with all due respect to him. Because I think at times we've discussed things that I felt were somewhat borderline when the witness is here. But I'd like to at least answer that question directly without him being present if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we proceed this way, that you probably continue with another line of question, and then immediately after the break, we discuss the issue of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayhew. With respect to your military background, sir, you discussed it in brief yesterday, and I read it within your statement. Can you share with us, sir, if at any time during your military training and background you ever took any instruction or commands from a civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at my junior level, I will be commanded normally by a more senior officer. In the end, the military will be responsible to a civilian government, but not at my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the military, sir, under any circumstance is responsible to a local community leader in an area when, in fact, as stated in your testimony yesterday, there was a new republic being formed or attempted to be formed by Mr. Radic from Banja Luka and others as we know, do you think that a local leader would have any influence over a military, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the British army, not normally. There are occasions when that would be the case, when the military are providing aid to the civil power and there is a legal framework under which that is done in times of natural disaster and in other circumstances. The systems differ around the world. I've seen a number of armies functioning, and I have had direct experience in other countries of armies working or military groups working under command directly of a civilian within the governing structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the incident that we referred to as the incident at Hambarine on May 22nd, are you, sir, familiar with an incident that occurred at the village or the town, I should say, of Kozarac on May 24th, 1992, a couple of days after the Hambarine incident, and again a couple of days before the implementation of this agreement that we've seen on annex D that we were briefly discussing earlier? Are you aware of that incident at all?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it now. However, if we were aware of it, I would expect it to show in the daily summary reports of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But all your daily summary reports are not provided to us, are they?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You saw all of them yesterday. Did you see a report that you had which talked about a military convoy that was passing through on the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just finish the question.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's okay. I may even change it at times at the end, so we have to be a little careful. Do you remember, sir, a report regarding a military convoy that was passing on the road, of the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road, and it was attacked specifically in the area known as Kozarac on or about May 24th, 1992 wherein several soldiers on the very first convoy were killed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. Again, it's of no surprise to me. I was dealing with a complex situation, many events around the region, reporting many such violent incidents every day. Ten years later, I'm most unlikely to remember it, unless my memory is refreshed by the relevant reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What effect in your opinion, if any, would an attack on the military convoy have on May 24th to the people in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would increase fear, it would increase anger, it would increase tension between the communities. Are you asking only about its effect on civilians or on others?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At this time only on the civilians. We'll talk about the military. My next question is about the military.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my answer then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What effect would it have, because the report clearly indicates, with respect to your interviews with several of the prisoners in the Trnopolje camp, that you discussed with them this May 24th attack on Kozarac and that, in fact, some of the witnesses told you the military attacked them and within 30 hours, I believe your report states, that they started looting the homes, evacuating the people from the area, burning the homes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, would it be possible for me to see the report? I remember it now, this is my conversation in Trnopolje relating to how people left their homes. It would be helpful for me to see that, if that's all right with the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have no objection. Let me just find it. Just let me direct his attention to it, if I may. For the Court and perhaps the Registrar has this as an exhibit, this is the report --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 215. Exhibit 215.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Exhibit S215, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is that the report which on the first page has Manjaca and Trnopolje identified?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if you go down to the section on page 2 of that report, under "Trnopolje," I think there's a brief discussion of the open reception centre as identified in the first sentence, then four paragraphs below, under the caption "Trnopolje," I think it discusses interviews with witnesses, et cetera. And if you can take an opportunity now to review that, and I have some questions on that.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's true if you flip on the next page that this is your report?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It has that caveat on it, which we'll talk about a little bit. I know it was mentioned yesterday. With respect to this paragraph, did you verify, sir, as to whether or not the military actually took 30 hours in order to evacuate, loot, and to burn the homes in the Kozarac area, on or about May 24th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And as I explained in the text, this is a reported conversation. It's a claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if at any time the military contacted the local leaders, after having sustained an attack during this convoy trip on the Prijedor/Banja Luka in order to ask the local authorities once their own military personnel were shot - I'm asking you to assume that - what they should do in response?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you have my report here. And if I had known further facts, I would have reported them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, as your job on this mission, did you try to obtain any other facts to know what led to this military attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and the reason for that was we were escorting a team in. Our job was to facilitate their visit, and we had no liberty to, because of the programme that was set, to go off and begin our work again. In addition, we had no authorisation from either our mission or from the Bosnian-Serb authorities to be doing our work. We only had authorisation for this specific visit, in which I was a facilitator.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, based on your experience and your presence in Bosnia in 1992, would you agree with me that it's highly unlikely that a military commander, whichever position he may hold, if attacked - and we're going to assume he's being attacked - if he sustained some deaths on his military personnel, would it be highly unlikely that that military command would call a local leader in the town and ask him how he should respond to the attack?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military leader would be highly unlikely to ask advice, if that's your question, from a civilian leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Under that scenario and even scenarios less tragic than those that we have described, based upon that assumption that they occurred. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what I'm asking -- my previous response was he would be highly unlikely to ask for advice from a civilian leader from whose town of the opposite ethnic group, that's what I'm referring to. So in the case of Kozarac, to ask advice from the civilian leader from whose population the military commander thinks the attack may have come, that's the person he's highly unlikely to ask. Was your question about that, or was it about any civilian leader?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any civilian leader. The military which was passing through, whether they are a federal military unit, a republic military unit, would they, while they are being attacked within that 24 to 30-hour period actually call and contact the local leaders of Prijedor in order to determine what, if anything, they should do?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends entirely on the relationship that they have with them. If they have a classical military command structure which goes up, say, to a defence council before reaching any civilian authority, then it would be highly unlikely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For certain reasons, not only for the reason just given, I think it's appropriate to have a break now. And I want to recall that the one or other party asked the Bench in the past to intervene when a witness starts to display his own opinion in a very broad level and where the Judges would be interested to what extent the opinion given here is fact-based. And of course, we have a fact witness before us. I know you would say that in the past, we had some other problems. But please be aware when discussing these issues during the last days, we also learn lessons, also from motions of the parties, we will no longer tolerate hypothetical questions on opinions of witnesses which appear here as mere fact witnesses. The trial stands adjourned until 10 minutes past 4.00. And then we restart without the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. We agreed that we want to discuss the relevance of the question of the killing of a colleague of the witness during the absence of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that opportunity. It's uncertain because we don't have the report what effect, if any, the killing of this colleague and person who came to investigate and to assist in the tensions that were growing in the area in Bosnia. However, I think it's logical to conclude that it may have an impact when a colleague of yours is killed, as he put it, murdered, on his further duties and responsibilities in the region. Although I don't want to speculate to that, but it certainly goes and the rules provide that it may go to bias, prejudice, or in some fashion the reports that were provided subsequent to the killing and those that were provided prior to the killing. Without having that, it's impossible for us to put it in proper context other than to speculate that it may be. Further to that, if this witness is testifying that it was a Serb or Serb authorities, I think it's relevant because it happened in May of 1992. It was an area in, I think the OTP concedes and identifies in his report, was in Mostar controlled by the Muslims and the Croatians at the time. And if it's his belief, it was the Serbian forces, whether it's the JNA or any other entity like that, because I understood from my learned colleague that in his statement it says it was an JNA personnel who did the killing, it may, in our opinion, have an impact on his credibility and his reports that were prepared in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any observations in addition to this? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think there's anything I can say that isn't clear to Your Honour already. This is, in our submission, just nonsense. The inquiry held into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Into the death of an ECMM monitor in Mostar in May of 1992 can be relevant to the credibility of this witness we say is errant nonsense. But it's up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that we don't share your language. But to be serious, some remarks seem to be necessary, because the word "relevance" seems to become a word of a foreign language in this courtroom more and more. In the past, we were hesitant to intervene here and there because it would stop the flow of information. And recapitulating the last witnesses, starting, say, with Witness Sejmenovic, the Judges have some doubt if it's really necessary to hear witnesses in this unlimited way, introducing especially documents far away from the witness before us through the witness. Because doing so, no doubt, it opens Pandora's box for the other party, because then everything also, all the parts of the documents, form part of the examination-in-chief, and the Judges have no possibility to intervene when some documents or some parts of the documents are contested. And the last witness before us, really to emphasise all these points of our major concern, it was announced one and a half hour, and our assessment was this witness could have been heard in one and a half hour. It took us two days. Once again, with the witness before us, we have this, no doubt, important document. In our point of view, this document could have been presented as a document as such, as all the other documents introduced into this case. And I wonder why it's necessary to face the witness with the question: "Does this comply with that what you experienced at that time in the area?" Can you really expect a witness telling us that he disagrees with what that was written down by his superiors? When we discussed the question whether or not this witness should be heard as a live witness, the basis was, as it was -- as it can be found in the witness summary 59, it states: "In August 1992, he met with Milomir Stakic in Prijedor who stated that Muslims were detained for their own safety." Maybe I'm wrong, but I couldn't see anything about this issue which was the reason why we said it would be appropriate to hear this witness as a live witness, anything about it in the transcript. And this was included in the summary of the OTP. Therefore, we want to ask both parties to concentrate on the relevant issues; and in doing so, probably not proceed introducing documents through a witness. It may be that sometimes it's of assistance that an already introduced document will be presented to a witness, and on this basis, of course, questions can be put to this witness. But not to introduce through a witness because once again, also in the case before us, having introduced the entire document on the report of the CSCE mission to inspect missions of places of detention of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 29 August to 4 August, once again, it opens Pandora's box for all the questions for all the areas contained in this report. And I can't see any legal basis to stop the Defence to ask, from our point of view, irrelevant questions because they are included in this report. Nevertheless, I would ask of the Defence in this case, put it this way, to come down to earth. It's not for me to evaluate at this point in time the relevance of the witness's testimony. But it could be that the testimony as such is relatively -- has relatively limited probative value, and therefore, I don't believe that in the concrete case, we are seized now with, it's necessary and it's relevant to ask all the questions on this killing or murder. It happened evidently far, far -- far, far would be the wrong word, but not in the area of our fourth amended indictment. And therefore, indeed, we can't see - we discussed it during the break - any relevance in this respect. And therefore, we would ask you to refrain from touching upon this area of this killing of this person. And please, try to show from your side some self-restraint and address those questions really relevant on the basis of the fourth amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I really ought to make some comment about what Your Honour has just said. The first is this: We weren't aware why Your Honours wanted to hear it, except obviously from the point of view that he met Stakic. But all that he could say is what is contained in the evidence of that meeting note made by Mr. McLeod. That's why I didn't take him through it again. Secondly, Your Honour, the report of the mission, firstly, they are not his superiors. He was sent as a guide to this mission, but they are, in no sense, his superiors. The report relates directly to things he witnessed in part and did seem to us that a report on Trnopolje and the like is relevant to this case. Now, I could have of course excised all the parts that don't bear on it, but it seemed to me that it was preferable that the whole report went before Your Honours with only the parts that were relevant being read. Can I say finally this, on this matter. If Your Honours feel that evidence we are calling is not relevant, then if Your Honours would indicate that and then perhaps hear our argument on it, or submissions, then we would know where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The reasons for hearing the witness before us, I just stated. And I'm afraid it is not an evaluation and no comment, but the very short summary seems, to a certain extent, misleading based on the answers we received yesterday. Ask it is only very limited evidence we have really related to Dr. Stakic, and people having seen, heard, spoken with Dr. Stakic. And therefore, it is necessary to hear everybody available for these purposes. As regards the second issue, of course that what the witness -- last witness had to tell us was relevant, but the way it is presented, over two days, that's our concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In chief, Your Honour, he finished in three hours or whatever yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no. The witness before, when we had the odyssey from one point to the other where the witness found corpses and collected these corpses. And we discussed this in depth and came to the conclusion this could have been done indeed, as it was indicated on the summary, within one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take full responsibility for that. I'm sorry. My instructions to Ms. Sutherland were that the details should be gone into, so that is entirely my responsibility, and -- it's not Ms. Sutherland's fault; it's my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not the question to apologise. It is only the question how to proceed in future, and when we are confronted and this witness has made all efforts to come here to The Hague, I think it is also understandable from the point of view of the accused and the Defence, that the Judges can't interfere and say, as it would be normal in a criminal court: "It's no longer relevant, and thank you for your information." Because there, we have to take into account our peacekeeping mission, and this means also to hear a witness coming here to The Hague on issues which are not directly relevant for the case before us, because it's a story the witness has to tell us from his own suffering and his own experience. But I would ask the parties, both parties in future, really, to concentrate on the main and the core issues of this case. Otherwise, we run out of the limits given indeed by the relevance as to the fourth amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, thank you, and obviously the Defence respects the ruling and the decision by the Court. However, we are placed in a somewhat difficult situation when witnesses do appear, we, the Defence, and particularly myself, seem to be offered some constructive criticism by my learned friends of the OTP. They suggest quite vehemently that we should present our evidence during the period of time at which we're conducting our cross-examination under Rule 90(H). When we try to do that, they scream and yell it's not relevant. We think respectfully that the events in the surrounding areas within the relevant time period are necessary for purposes of establishing a complete picture. It also, without going into the detail, may have impact, I personally believe it has a great impact, on some of the witnesses that the OTP has called, specifically the very first witness they called when the trial commenced on the 16th of April of this year. My next point is that this is a document that we saw here which references a meeting that was held in The Hague in 1991. I agree that it is, from the scope of time, somewhat far afield from the time of the indictment. However, there's an exhibit that the Court marked after we withdrew it that counsel raised an issue as to its authenticity because that very meeting was mentioned in the SDA minutes. And from that, one would think that the minutes were created subsequent as opposed to contemporaneous with the meeting being held, and then we learn now, despite the OTP's strenuous objection saying it was offered by Defence counsel in another case and that were questions raised about the authenticity about that document, The Hague and the United Nations were indeed involved at least seemingly so from some of these documents, as early as November 1991. And this is an opportunity that we have from this witness who was briefed on these matters to enlighten us on the exhibit that was marked I think as J3, I believe -- I believe that's the document, I could get that to verify it. And again it doesn't necessarily go specifically to our defence. That document has been discussed. We didn't offer it into evidence. It was provided to us. They thought it was shed some light on the meetings and the parties involved, namely the SDA. So we asked a question on that. I certainly will not ask any questions any more, and I understand the Court's ruling on that with respect to the monitor but we have other issues that are raised specifically in this report that I must ask the witness. I expect fully to conclude today in ample time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you understood from our remark that the document as such is, of course, of importance, and indeed, the -- I don't believe that it's contested in this courtroom that the period immediately, say, from the end of 1990 onwards is, of course, relevant for the case. And on the basis of this, I believe we can continue now. And may the witness be brought in again. But please, remember your own words on opinion witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence may then proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayhew. Sir, if I can just back up a little bit and ask you a question with respect to the procedure that you followed in April and May of 1992 while in Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily in the Prijedor area, was it your policy and practice, sir, to take notes and to keep daily recordation of meetings that you had with various ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we would take notes during the meetings and translate the relevant parts of them into our reports back to Zagreb via the regional centre in Sarajevo. My own personal practice was to keep a minimum of notes after that, after they had been used for the purpose of the evening report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would there be any scenario where you had a meeting with let's say all three of the ethnic groups in Prijedor in April and May of 1992 where notes of that meeting or a report summarising that meeting would not have been made?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't imagine it, unless by chance it was an ad hoc meeting, very short and insubstantial on the roadside because of a chance meeting. But I don't recall any such occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It would be a highly unlikely that you would have a roadside meeting with all three ethnic groups. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 14 of yesterday's transcript, you discuss a meeting that was held in April and May, line -- page 14, line 9 through 19 is the essence of that. You state there that "at that point, in April, May, we met with the council of the district, and in particular the three leaders of the three ethnic groups within the council, including the mayor." Just to put it in perspective for you. Do you, as you sit here today, sir, recall having a meeting in April and May in Prijedor in 1992 with the three ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the wording you just read out from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you, sir, have -- is it fair to say, sir, there exists or to your knowledge would there exist a report which describes in detail what was said at the various groups at that meeting in April or May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is almost certainly -- there is almost certainly a report of that meeting. How much detail it went into in the official report, I'm not sure. It might -- we might have judged it, part of the ongoing dialogue, and therefore not necessary to report in detail. But it is a more or less unthinkable that we would not describe that meeting to some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. extent in our official report of that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In preparation for your testimony here, do you recall reviewing that report at the end of that meeting with those three ethnic groups in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid as you've already noticed, I have read a number of reports both ten years ago and just recently. Yes, I have read - you're quite right - I have read a report by Charles McLeod of at least one such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall in that report whether or not there was a discussion as to who was present and what was said?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be helpful for me at this point to have in front of me any such report that's available to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, sir, if --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think there is some confusion. As I explained with Mr. McLeod, we were depending on what ECMM could find from its archives. I think there's confusion between the two meetings because as far as I know, Mr. Mayhew has not seen any report, through us, that relates to a meeting held before he left in May. So McLeod reports are all the ones at the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this, Mr. Mayhew, if you may, who was it that determined when you left the Zagreb or Croatian front line and moved to the Bosnian and the Serb area, who decided that the three important places which you would visit would be Banja Luka, Prijedor, and Derventa?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been a decision made in Banja Luka by the team whose leader at that time, I think, was Dave Holt [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what the basis of selecting Prijedor as one of the three areas was?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I can guess intelligently if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, the Court, I believe, or at least typically, we don't like people to guess, and we don't like speculation, or at least I don't. So to the extent that you wish to tell us, if you have a reasonable basis for it, you can share that with us. But I hesitate to inquire further of a question when it's followed by an answer involving either speculation or guess. So perhaps I should restate the question. If you have a reasonable understanding as to the basis why Prijedor was selected, you could share that with us if you may.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious when you study the area that there are major centres of population. And it would be a sensible practice, in any such mission, to go to the major centres of population and start by focussing on those which have worse tensions than the others, and which are accessible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that in April and May of 1992, as you sit here, you do not recall any significant exchanges, in fact, no exchanges with military commanders in Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me think about that for a moment. I do not recall any exchanges with military commanders in the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And again --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I would be corrected by reports, as usual. If I wrote it, then it will be an accurate report of what happened. So if you find a report which says I did, then that will refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the period of time that we're discussing, sir, is April and May of 1992, just so that we're clear. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that the reason that there was no significant or any exchanges whatsoever with the military commanders in Prijedor area in April and May of 1992 was because at that stage, any potential crisis in the Prijedor area was merely a political one and did not involve the military at all?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it was primarily a political one. The military, of course, were becoming involved in events generally across the north Bosnia area. But the reason for our focussing on political meetings was that it was indeed a primarily political problem at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you, sir, have a date at which the time period in which you left the Bosnian area or the Prijedor area in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The record will have to remind me of the date that we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the time period that you were there in April and May of 1992, did you experience or see or do you have any comments relating to violence in Prijedor, having been broken out, or breaking out?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were told in that meeting with the council of some violence, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it would be wise to refer to the record. As I recall, all three sides wished to make it known that the other -- one other side or both other sides were primarily responsible for any increase in tension or violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, then let's check the record if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can have the Court instruct the usher to provide the witness with his statement dated March 14th through 15th, 2000, starting with the Bate stamp 00928862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may remind the witness and the counsel to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Directing your attention, sir, to page 4 of your report which has two ERN numbers on the top right-hand corner, one is numbered 00928865, and the other Bate stamp, ERN number is reflected as being 02120714.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: My copy only has the first of those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And directing your attention, sir, to the third full paragraph on page 4 of your witness statement, and there on the last sentence it states, at least in March of 2000, that you were unable to comment on the violence in Prijedor as: "I was no longer involved in Prijedor by the time that violence had broken out there." Can you share with us, sir, whether the statement that you provided to the OTP in March of 2000 is accurate in connection with this specific sentence or that which you shared with us moments ago, that you did recall that violence in Prijedor was present, or at least allegations were made of it, can you tell us which one of those two is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are both accurate, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to comment on the violence in Prijedor as I was no longer involved in Prijedor by the time that violence had broken out there. This statement means that I'm referring to serious major acts of violence, that's to say, essentially, the beginnings of a war. And I was no longer involved in Prijedor by the time that that kind of violence had broken out there. My statement of a moment ago is also accurate that it was reported to us, as I recall, in that council meeting that there had been some small and isolated acts of violence which were nevertheless politically significant. And we took note that that had happened.
