But such small acts involving maybe very small numbers of people were so common throughout the area, even before then, that I didn't describe that, I didn't include that in my word "violence" on page 4 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier today you also told us that with respect to having exchanges with the military commanders in the Prijedor area, and it being in fact a political crisis, if you will, as opposed to a military crisis, and then you shared with us on page 16 of your testimony yesterday, page 4, that the problem was primarily a political problem -- line 4 -- it was becoming a military problem, or became later a military problem. And so it was natural that we should go to the political leaders first." On line 6 of the transcript yesterday. If you compare that with the paragraph immediately preceding paragraph 3 on page 4 that you have before you, where in fact you state - it's in the second sentence of that second paragraph - that the reason that there were not -- you don't recall any significant exchanges with military commanders in the Banja Luka and Prijedor areas in April and May of 1992, or early May, was that "at that stage, the crisis was not a military one, but rather a political one." Is your testimony now, sir, that it was primarily a political problem and your statement of the year 2000 seems to indicate it was clearly a political problem and not involving the military at all. And if you can help me reconcile the two.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two are easily reconcilable. There is a short sentence on page 4 of my report which does not expand or go into detail or explain. It does not say it was "merely" or "only" or "clearly," to use your word just now, a political one. It says it was not a military, but rather political. That's not a claim of exclusivity, and it is clearly consistent with my more expanded remarks elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, I believe you told us that you were unaware of any political takeover by the SDS at the end of April 1992. Nowhere in your report can I find that you discuss there was a political takeover by any ethnic group of the Municipal Assembly during that time period. Can you tell us why not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we were aware at the time of a political takeover, we would, again, 99 per cent certainty have included it in our reports. So if there is a report in existence which would have -- which describes that, then we were aware of it. As I mentioned earlier, it appears that not every daily report is in the possession of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Put that aside for a moment. On page 22 of yesterday's transcript, lines 10 through 13, you were asked specifically whether or not you were aware at any stage before you left in May of a takeover that had occurred in Prijedor by the SDS. The answer, on page 22, line 13: "I don't remember that." My question to you, sir, is this: I don't see it in any of the reports. Is it your testimony that the Muslims and the political group that represented the Muslim community, the SDA party, that you claim you met with in April and May of 1992 would not have found that to be a significant event and would not have, therefore, shared that event with you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there had been a political takeover, and if we had met with the Muslim leadership, quite clearly, it would have been something they would have told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not if you met; you told us you met with all three ethnic groups. Right? There's no doubt about that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I clarify my remarks, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not in the record from that meeting, then it hadn't happened by that meeting, or most certainly. What I meant was if we had met subsequently with the Muslim leader, which was your question, you didn't ask subsequently, but if we had met with a Muslim leader including any other time, of course they would have told us and we would have been aware probably through other channels also.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But as you sit here, you don't have a recollection of that takeover occurring; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mention on page 14, as we previously cited, that there was a meeting in April and May with the council of the district. Can you describe for me what it is that you coin as "council of the district" on page 14, line 10?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the precise name of the body. I do recall that it contained the mayor of Prijedor and his council. Now the precise nature of that body, I'm afraid it's too long ago for me to be able to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of that individual mayor and any of the participants who were in this council that you met with?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that in Prijedor and in any village or town or city in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 there existed no such entity as a "mayor" of a town? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijedor can be used either to describe the town or the municipality in which it lies. If what you say is true, then the mayor of Prijedor presumably refers to the mayor of Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that there is no such provision in any statute or law which has a position for "mayor" of Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that the exact terms and descriptions, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me if subsequent to this meeting in April and May of 1992 you held any other meetings with any members of the Muslim ethnic group? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very likely that we did. We were always trying to meet with a representative sample of all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here, sir, do you remember on how many occasions subsequent to this meeting where all three ethnic groups were represented, how many times you would have met with Muslim representatives, exclusively?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea whether it was more than one, or can you as you sit here only think of one?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember because the details of our daily work are now a matter of record, rather than my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: After leaving the region in May of 1992, you were stationed back in Zagreb or in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: After May 1992, back in Zagreb for most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During that time period, sir, did you do any work at all, related to the area of Prijedor Municipality, even though you were distantly and physically removed from the area?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued to follow the Bosnian reports from the whole of Bosnia, including all parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From whom would you receive any such reports that you would be following?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ECMM monitor teams had evacuated. And until later on, and I don't remember the exact date, we had no ECMM source of information from within Bosnia. However, we actively built up links with other international organisations, and we tried to keep in touch with the situation through those and any other means, including the press that were available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you have maintained your relationships with the various ethnic groups that you had previously met in the Prijedor region?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to retain communications with everyone as far as communications allowed. And I do not recall, in detail, the people with whom we were able to remain in contact. But I do recall that our contacts were very restricted indeed, to the extent that we had difficulty sometimes contacting the Banja Luka authorities. And I think it was even harder still to be in contact with others who were less easy to communicate with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you aware during your time in the Prijedor Municipality in April and May of 1992 whether there was approximately seven to 10.000 Serbian refugees that were in the area of Trnopolje and the town of Prijedor who came from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't remember about that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that that's a significant number, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by detail, I mean not that it's insignificant, I simply mean that that is one of the many facts we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, sir, did you verify the fact that the Croatians expelled and displaced seven to 10.000 Serbs from Croatia and its borders, and that those seven to 10.000 found their way in the Prijedor Municipality? Did you try to verify that fact at any time?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly verified many expulsions of Serb civilians from Croatia, and where we could, we tried to follow the subsequent events. But our primary concern was to report on the fact of expulsion, and our resources did not permit us to follow in most cases, as I recall, the destination of each group because there were many people going in many, many directions. And we did it -- so I can't comment on that group. But I do recall much investigation of expulsions from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this, if you can: If you were and part of your duties was to go in the Prijedor area and to -- although a complex situation as you yourself described- to have a complete understanding of the situation and to have an appreciation for all three ethnic sides, did you at any time, sir, interview any of the refugees that were in the Prijedor Municipality in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Again, that's for our daily work. We would have tried to do so. Our time was limited. The situation was breaking down. And so as I mentioned earlier, we had to ruthlessly prioritise our work, so as to be certain that we had the maximum possible effect on the whole situation. And that meant prioritising the leaders on all three sides and keeping informed where time permitted with random visits or premeditated visits to ordinary families, including refugee families.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was your impression, if any, at that time as to the influx or these refugees that came from Croatia, Serbian refugees, in the Municipality of Prijedor? What effect, if any, did they have on the political situation that was existing in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the effect of that particular group, as I have explained. But the overall effect of Serb refugees arriving was to cause stress and fear and dismay among the Serb population from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you at any time, sir, come across a scenario where some of these refugees, if you will, who came acted in a revenge against the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As a result of actually being kicked out and expelled from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like, if I may, to turn now to this provisionally identified exhibit that you should still have in front of you, S217, please. I'll try to limit it to the parts that you read, although you read --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I make a comment on that, please, to the Court. I'd like to just apologise for my momentary earlier confusion on the question of the parts of the CSCE report and to clarify that since the only part that I now realise -- the only part that I had not read was an attached document containing the text of an ICRC agreement, my comments on the report do apply to all parts of the report written by the CSCE team.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you turn to Part I of that report, paragraph number 2, which is approximately the fifth page or so. It has the ERN number 00999576, second paragraph, the middle section of that paragraph: "On the contrary, we are unanimous that we saw only part of the picture, but we did see a lot and spoke with many people including some hundreds of prisoners. We are aware that the picture, as we saw it, is subject to fluctuation." Do you agree or disagree with that statement in the report?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me what it means when they say: "is subject to fluctuation"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've mentioned already that the situation was fast changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's what it means?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask the authors for a fuller explanation. I would guess that that is a major part of what it means, but I thought you didn't like me to guess. I can -- I mean, "fluctuation" in this context is, of course, referring to the fluctuation in the situation of detention centres, which of course relate closely to the fluctuation or the changing circumstances outside those centres. And it's a matter of record that the numbers of people in those centres -- numbers of people in those centres did change.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It also states that you or the group "interviewed hundreds of prisoners." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me with respect to the Prijedor Municipality and the camps that were alleged to have been established there, namely Trnopolje, can you tell me how many prisoners in Trnopolje were actually interviewed by you or the CSCE?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: CSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for the exact number of detainees interviewed by the CSCE mission because we all split up and fanned out through the camp. Myself, I spoke to approximately -- of the order of 6 to 15 members of the camp, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At the Trnopolje camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many prisoners did you interview who were in the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was your answer relating to you personally or to the entire group?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that myself, I spoke to between 6 and 15 at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Manjaca yourself. We're only interested to learn your personal observations and experiences while you were there at that time. How many would you have interviewed?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 4, possibly a few more than 4. And the nature of those interviews was very different. Snatched conversations out of earshot of the guards which was only possible for, say, 30 seconds at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long, while you were at Trnopolje, how long did your visit at the Trnopolje camp take? A day, two days?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. No, it was within one day. But it was a matter of, let us say, one to two hours approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if the visit to Trnopolje followed the visit to the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have the document here. May I refer to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where it's stated?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't recall, at the moment. Maybe just to speed it along, just accept it as true, and my learned friend will object and clarify it. I'm not trying to mislead you on it. That's my recollection of how the process went.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll accept what the report says. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Trnopolje camp and the Manjaca military camp were strikingly different in many respects? One, at Manjaca, there was a barbed wire fence. At Trnopolje, there was not a barbed wire fence.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, are you pausing, or is that the end of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: End of that part of the question, there are other subsections within that question.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We noticed that the barbed wire fence had been recently removed from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time, sir, investigate when the barbed wire -- are you saying it was a barbed wire fence or just a wire fence? Because in your report you never mention, and we can look through your report, that there was ever a barbed wire fence at Trnopolje. As you sit here, I want your recollection as to whether or not you believe there was a barbed wire fence at Trnopolje that surrounded the entire school or compound?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've mentioned, the fence was not there once we arrived. And therefore, I couldn't tell you whether it was a barbed wire or wire. It would be unusual a camp to have wire other than barbed wire, which is why I mentioned barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it be unusual, sir, for witnesses to claim that they actually entered and exited Trnopolje camp in July and August 1992 on numerous occasions if there were barbed wire fence being surrounding the entire complex? That would truly be an unbelievable thing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it a hypothetical question? Therefore, please, either rephrase or...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you expect, sir, that a person can get in and out of the camp by slipping through or between the barbed wire fencing if in fact it's true that Trnopolje, that there existed barbed wire fence surrounding the entire centre?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pausing for the.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Again, it's still a hypothetical question, what somebody could or could not do, whether there was or not barbed wire. This witness can't really assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 90(H), Your Honour, and I don't want to quote my opposing counsel at all, requires us to put facts at issue if we deem that they are relevant. And in fact, if I recall, counsel was adamant in instructing us and lecturing me on how the rule should be applied. And in every instance if there's an occasion that we could provide a defence which may go to any of the issues, they invited us to present that to the witness. We're simply providing that. It's not a hypothetical. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness has clearly stated that he hasn't seen a fence or barbed wire fence or whatsoever fence. And you wanted to lay it in the direction of fence totally around this, we have heard a lot of evidence on this. I think it was clear enough the answer the witness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hasn't seen such a fence. Full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Also, when you look at the striking difference between Manjaca camp and Trnopolje, did you ever learn that in Trnopolje, there was a watch tower with watch guards securing the area in Trnopolje, whereas in Manjaca, as you clearly state, there was a watch tower and security was actually very intense?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've reported that there were guard posts, ground-level guard posts, not a tower, at Trnopolje. I don't remember a tower, and if my report doesn't state one, it is probable that there was not one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In Manjaca, when you visited it, there were German shepherds also in the camp. Do you remember hearing from the prisoners who shared with you, that there were no such guard dogs every present?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 6 to 15 interviewees. I don't remember any conversation about dogs with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: Is it your testimony that Trnopolje and Manjaca were the same in both the way security was provided and both the way the camp was set up, or were they different?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Strikingly different, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, particularly in the question of access, and in the demeanour of the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Expand on what you mean when you say: "particularly with respect to access"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've covered it in my answer about the fence. We were not -- the reports mention accounts of who could leave the camp and who could stay. And to my recollection, those reports are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in Trnopolje, family and friends were permitted to visit the members within the camp and were allowed to bring in food, water, clothing supplies, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that not yet another striking difference between the Trnopolje centre and the Manjaca military camp?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. The reason I hesitate is that I can't be completely certain in my memory that no relatives could visit Manjaca camp. Again, the report will remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 13 of the CSCE mission report which has the Bate stamp number 00999584, and the bottom portion discusses the ICRC and family visits. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does it mention there anywhere that, in fact, in other camps, family and friends were permitted to visit, or does it clearly state: "With the exception of Trnopolje and perhaps one or two other camps and centres, families and friends are not permitted to visit."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does state what you say it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have an independent recollection, sir, as to whether or not family and friends were permitted to visit detainees at the Manjaca military camp?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I have already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn to an annex, annex B of the report, just for purposes of clarification, I have a couple questions in connection with this annex B. Let me know when you've reached that point, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm at that page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the camps that are listed which contain Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you know if there was any verification done by your team or the CSCE to verify whether or not those camps existed where Serbs were held as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was at least one visit, and I imagine possibly a number of others by ECMM staff to a camp containing Serb civilian prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name of the place. But I remember seeing the report, including possibly one of the reports that the Court has seen. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at that second page of that annex B and look down at the prison in Sarajevo which states or, in essence, states that about 600 Serbs were confined there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What does that mean in parenthesis after that paragraph when it says "confirmed"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine it means that the CSCE team had confirmed that themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you help me with this: What's the date that it was confirmed, or the date in which these Serbs were held prisoner in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list given by Mr. Karadzic, according to page 20, the first page of the annex, to the CSCE mission. And therefore, it is likely to mean that at the date when Mr. Karadzic handed over this list, those Serbs were believed by him to be in detention and confirmed, I'm assuming, by the team, though possibly through -- well, it's possible that they had asked the ICRC and the ICRC had confirmed that. But the ICRC may have refused to confirm or deny that. So that is why I think it probable that the team had confirmed with their own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me that it's more than just a possibility; it's more likely than not, since it has in parenthesis under these prison camps in Sarajevo with Serbs captured in them that it puts confirmed that indeed they verified the existence of that camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was a possibility, but probable. And it certainly means that they verified it to their satisfaction that those Serbs were in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Having been in Zagreb and Prijedor, did you confirm or at any time try to verify the existence of this fact that Serb civilians were held in prison in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a confirmation of Sarajevo prisoners by the ECMM. At the time of this report, of course, it was no longer necessary because it had been independently verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you flip to the next page, sir, which has the Bate stamp number 00999593, and I'm really directing your attention to the last portion of that where again they discuss 600 Serbs captured in the central prison in Sarajevo. Do you see that? Three lines from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say who the commander of the camp; and then it identifies them both as being a senior and also prominent member of the SDA which is the Democratic Action Party of the Muslim ethnic group. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was also a representative in the assembly of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina which follows on the next page of that document. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, from this report - it's difficult for me to understand - whether that was in fact verified that the commander of the camp was Safet Isovic or this was an allegation that someone called Safet Isovic was the camp commander where 600 Serb civilians were held?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't immediately see for sure which of the two options is the case. The heading of that section is that this is a list given by Mr. Karadzic, and it's not clear from a quick reading just now whether this final paragraph of Section 1 is a comment by the team or a reported claim by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Following on that page, meaning that next page, it discusses 6.000 Serbs being killed, and that concentration camps were established by a Croatian/Muslim coalition, and the numbers increased every day. Most of them captured are women and children. Based on your duties, sir, there, do you recall ever being briefed about that fact or that issue?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it, but we would have received a copy of this report, and it would have been read within the mission and probably read by myself, although I can't be completely certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As you sit here, do you know how many camps this Croatian/Muslim coalition established and when?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this Croatian/Muslim coalition established any camps in the first quarter of 1992, namely, January, February, and March?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I would have to defer to reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you can return to annex C, please. Annex C, sir - and you're welcome to read the entire thing because you've also told us you already reviewed it - it discusses the long-term hopes of some of the people that were interviewed by the CSCE mission. As you can see on that second paragraph, the last full sentence, do you agree with that, sir, that "no one wishes in present circumstances to return to their homes in Western Bosnia because the local administration cannot and will not guarantee their physical security."

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this, when you were interviewing and discussing with these detainees in Trnopolje, did they also express that to you, that they did not want to return home because they weren't given this guarantee?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact details, but this was my general impression from those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You discussed yesterday at page 30 of your testimony, some conclusions that were drawn, and specifically you state that you disagreed or who have preferred, I should say, my apologies, that the phrase "by whatever method is available," that that certainly was a quote that you would not have liked to use, but you would have like to have used a different quote, and that is "if the authorities truly wanted whatever method --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 30, Your Honour, I'm sorry line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- And if the authorities truly wanted whatever method, they could have already transported them to the border or taken other measures. So I would have probably replaced that phrase with something like `whatever method they could get away with' or and possible have allowed some room for a different of opinion among the Bosnian Serb leadership. After all, not everyone was certain that 100 per cent of the Muslim population had to go." And then you proceed. My question with respect to that, sir, is having been there, both in April and May of 1992, and returning to the area again in August and September of 1992, had the Serb authorities wanted to kick out, expel, even murder the detainees within the alleged camps that existed, what prevented them from doing that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I would be giving my opinion of their likely motivations. And is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We know --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this, sir, and maybe I'll rephrase the question. The Serbs were in control in the area at that time. If they had detained the individuals as you've identified in your reports and have testified here yesterday and today, what prevented them from expelling those individuals as you told us yesterday, what prevented them from doing that in early May, June, July, or August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had wanted to expel them all, physically, nothing prevented them. Politically, public opinion, world opinion prevented them. That is, if they wanted to. And as you've quoted my remarks yesterday, it was not clear to me that there was a unanimous single political vision. And there will have been disagreements among the authorities as to their aims. So it is questionable, highly questionable, if they wanted to. But I'm assuming that your question assumes if they wanted, what could have prevented them? And the answer is political, rather than physical.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know it's not a concern for you, but there's some allegations with respect to that, and that's why I'm asking you that. If the Serbian authorities wanted to or had the intent to commit mass massacres of the individuals they detained in these camps such as Trnopolje, what prevented them from doing it in May, June, July, and August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically, nothing. They had guns and the people didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They are people, too.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So, physically, nothing. It is physically possible. But politically, it would have been disastrous for them. And I am really hesitating here to enter into speculation as to their motivations. We all know that a humane person would never wish to do that. But I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so. Refrain from speculations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I hesitate to go further in answering the question as you seem to expect me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure, Your Honour, what time Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you'd like to take a break. It may be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayhew. If I can direct your attention, sir, again to the annex we were just discussing -- or previously discussing, which is annex B, I'll give you the ERN number, or, as I say, Bate stamp number 00999593, remember we talked about that Mr. Safet Isovic below. In the centre of that, or immediately above that reference, sir, there's a discussion of a chief investigator who was also purportedly involved in one of the camps that Serbian civilians were detained and were prisoners. It also proceeds to state: "Among others, there are 20 Arab guards." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. Where is this in the paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Immediately below the indented paragraph starting with "Sarajevo sport hall" and then approximately seven to 10 lines below that.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You were in the area during the period in question, namely, April through - in part - August, September 1992. Would you know if that reference to the 20 Arab guards is a reference to mercenaries who arrived in the Bosnia and Croatian territories in February of 1992 to assist the Muslims in their fight and battle?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anything about these Arab guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it be safe to state that when we referenced "20 Arab guards," clearly they are not referring to the Bosnian Muslims or the Croatian Muslims that lived in the former territory known as Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your job and during your duties there, did you ever hear a rumour or a report of these Arab mercenaries who came into either Bosnia or Croatia to help during the civil war that was taking place there?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were indeed reports and rumours of Middle Eastern Muslim mercenaries or fighters supplied to the Bosnian Muslim part of the coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you and your group do to verify that fact, or that rumour?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that we did anything, which would be natural, because we were excluded from Bosnia for almost all of that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the parties not to discuss rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, going back now, if I may, to the Trnopolje camp, on page 58 on your transcript yesterday, and just refreshing your recollection on that, specifically line 12, you answer a question on the organisation of the camps, particularly Trnopolje and Manjaca is what you're referencing there, and your answer is as follows: "Yes, there was firm clear organisation and chains of command evident, particularly at Manjaca, and also at Trnopolje. It was clear that the uniformed personnel were under clear command." Line 14. Taking that into account, if you can turn to the CSCE report where they discuss Trnopolje, specifically at ERN and Bate stamp number 00999619, under the discussion captioned "general conditions in Trnopolje" the very last sentence of that section it states: "This centre appears to have no real organisation and is undoubtedly `a disaster ready to happen'." Help me with this, sir, was the CSCE incorrect in saying that the centre had no real organisation or was the fact that there was no real organisation at Trnopolje? Which of the two statements would be accurate?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So they were organised and yet unorganised?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre having no real organisation appears to be a reference to the way that the internal part of the centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness, may I interrupt. Are you aware what you are saying here. You are clearly stating under solemn declaration that you know on the basis of facts that this centre had no organisation. Do you know this by facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said, Your Honour, was that this sentence appears to be saying that the centre had no organisation within it, and the reason I used the word "appears to be saying" was to make clear the fact that I am saying what it seems to be saying in the light of my knowledge of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct that you are not one of the authors of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And is it correct that what you are doing now is more or less guessing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in my opinion, I am interpreting the meaning of the report in response to a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you have any underlying facts bringing you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my knowledge of the ground, my presence that day, and my reports that I've sense refreshed my memory with. I think it might help Your Honour if I give the second part of what I was about to say which might make clear the response I was going to give which is dependent on fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It was already now the second time that I had to caution you, that you have to base what you are saying here on facts. And it's no doubt that the Defence has the right to put the question to you. But you're responsible for the answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to reconcile two sentences which the Defence points out may appear to some to be conflicting. So let me, then, perhaps explain what I meant by my statement about clear command and confine my remarks initially, my response initially to that. We were visiting Trnopolje in the company of the Bosnian Serb authorities. The military personnel, or uniformed personnel, they might have been paramilitary, I don't know, at Trnopolje were aware of our visit, and it is for that reason that I say that they were clearly under command because there could have been no official visit conducted in that manner, with the knowledge and accompaniment of the Bosnian Serb authorities, unless the soldiers were of the -- under command in a manner which they recognised. And it is for that reason that I stand by my statement. And I will with the Judges' direction to leave it to the Court to decide how to interpret the sentence in the CSCE report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Also in that section on the same page in the CSCE report, under the same section "General Conditions in Trnopolje" the first sentence states as follows: "We have been led to believe that the authority is relatively relaxed during the mornings and until 3.00 p.m. each afternoon when the major in charge completes his on-site duties." Did you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to that, just so I'm clear, it's a military personnel with a rank of major, correct, it's not to be confused with what you've coined previously in the meetings that you have had with a mayor, having the Y instead of the J. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been cautioned on commenting on what this report means. The word "major" in English cannot be confused with the word "mayor" in English. But it may be a spelling mistake and I can't comment on whether this is a spelling mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You were there and based on whatever amount of time you were there, do you recall any discussion that actually the camp commander or the major who was in charge, whether he completed his on-site duties and was not on the premises after 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any such discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the second page or the next page of this annex that we're referring, which has the ERN number 00999620, it discusses and continues to discuss the conditions at Trnopolje and how some of the detainees there maintained contact with the outside world. If I may direct your attention to that next page, the very last paragraph. Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to that, do you recall ever discussing with the detainees or prisoners at Trnopolje camp what or how they made contact with the outside world?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall discussing that with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing or discussing with any of the detainees at the Trnopolje camp whether they were allowed to walk about the centre relatively freely, were given the opportunity to play chess, and engage in more lively conversations with their fellows?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I observed that, and I remember commenting on it in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know it was read to you, but I wasn't sure if you --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know if I conversed with them about that subject, but I was able to witness that they were doing those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention now back to your statement that you have in front of you dated March 14th and 15th, 2000, page 6, at the bottom of that statement, I'm focussing, if I may, your attention to the third full paragraph in connection with the topic of Bosanska Gradiska. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, who was the mayor of Bosanska Gradiska that you reference that you met on or about August 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with respect to that visit, you seem to have an impression, as you state yourself on the last sentence, that you had an impression both in April and May and August and September that the civilian authorities cooperated closely with the military authorities and the police. Is it fair to say, sir, that in light of that statement and that visit to Bosanska Gradiska, it is indeed limited to and only relates to Bosanska Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to April-May 1992, it would not be limited to Bosanska Gradiska because we were in frequent contact with many parts of the society there, including military and political. In respect of August-September 1992, I don't remember if we met military and civilians together outside that Bosanska Gradiska meeting except, of course, within Manjaca and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for me what the uniforms were of the personnel that were at the Trnopolje Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the uniforms that the personnel had that were at the Trnopolje Detention Centre, whether these uniforms were consistent with each and every member who was securing the facility? Were they uniform?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, who was the camp commander, if you will, or representative leader of the camp at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if you ever met that individual?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You state -- or it states on the CSCE report in describing Manjaca, following the aspect that we just discussed with respect to Trnopolje, that there were "German Shepherd guard dogs were seen patrolling the periphery of the centre, manned watchtowers were located at different points in the camp, and mines surrounded the camp and separated internal areas of the grounds." You can find that at ERN number 00999622 under the caption "Facility." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if Trnopolje during the 6 to 15 interviews that you conducted with the detainees there, whether any of them at any time informed or advised you that there were mines that surrounded the camp?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any of them making that claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If they had made that claim, you would have recorded it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Throughout both the CSCE report and your witness statement, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there's an estimate given of anywhere between 1.600 and 2.000 Muslim detainees that were kept in the Trnopolje camp. Various sections of this report, they mention the number 1.600. Did your or your group, sir, ever conduct a count of the detainees at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any organisation or institution which conducted a count of the detainees at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I'd like to seek the guidance of the judge at this point, bearing in mind his former cautions, that I can comment on what would be normal ICRC practice in such a case. But I wonder whether that would be permissible to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it is based on facts, no doubt you should do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the fact that it is normal ICRC practice to make lists, complete lists, of all places of detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen that list, sir, to determine whether the number that you cite in your witness statement and the report that's referenced in the CSCE report is accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never be permitted to see an ICRC list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of their internal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about their internal regulations that prohibit us from obtaining something that perhaps, individually, we would deem relevant? Do you know of anything that would prohibit us --

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Would you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll restate it.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Restate, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was an awkward question. I'd hate to repeat that one. What, to your knowledge, of the regulations of the ICRC would prohibit anyone from seeing the list of the individuals who were detained at Trnopolje camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are very discreet about all information to do with detainees. However, they do have to share lists sometimes when it is necessary, for example, to arrange a prisoner transfer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the ICRC report would also break down the gender, age, and composition of the people who were detained at an individual camp such as Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their internal practices in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask a clarification question on your note-taking and practices. We've heard from other witnesses and your colleagues, as you've heard Mr. McLeod, et cetera, did you at any time retain your handwritten notes of any of the meetings that you were present at in either April-May or at any time in August-September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: At about the time the 2000 interview, I did a search of my records, and I couldn't find any of my handwritten notes of any significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand. Why would you say "of any significance"? Did you find your notes or did you not find your notes, handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find any notes of meetings. And anything that I found -- I don't remember if I found anything, first of all. But anything that I found, if I did find something, was not pertinent to the case or to anything in my statement as it seemed to me. And I therefore gave it no further thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On this exhibit, S215, and I just have a couple questions on it, I know you touched upon it yesterday where it's a report dated -- generated by you dated September 4th, 1992, and you have the word "caveat" placed underneath. There's nothing under the word caveat, although I read the transcript and I am familiar, who deleted that section of your report and why?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of mission deleted it. And I don't know why. He thought that the report in this current form was more appropriate to send to London, and I'd like to just inform the Court of this point, because I think it's relevant, that I checked last night a diskette which I had brought with me on which some reports I didn't realise I had are. And I'm sorry for me remissness in not finding this before. But I did find this particular document of mine on the diskette in its full form, including the paragraph under "caveat." And I can submit that to the Court if you would like. The paragraph says that, from my memory, because we had not got the Serb side of the story during these visits from Trnopolje -- to Trnopolje and Manjaca, I advised caution and the document should be protected. I was very keen on impartial balance, as was important. I also mentioned in that paragraph that we had not had the chance to assess more widely across northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, sir, inquire, and if the Court permits -- if I may be permitted to inquire, sir, you also state that you found other reports on this diskette that you previously didn't see or didn't remember? Would that be kind of fair?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened was that -- sorry, first of all. There are other reports on the diskette. And I had not looked at the diskette until last night since my return from the Balkans nine years ago or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many reports -- how many reports are there that fit within the category that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The number.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Category?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two reports?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: The category that I've just described, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That you previously didn't know that you had and previously had not reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this diskette, I'm not sure, perhaps 20 reports. As I mentioned, I had done a search in 2000 because I live a nomadic existence and have only recently got married and settled down, all my effects have been dispersed. I did a final search just before coming here and found a couple of diskettes which were unclearly marked. I threw them in my luggage and then I'm afraid, forgot about their existence until last night. I checked them last night and found a number of reports dating from the ECMM. So they are now available to the Court, if you wish. All of them are to be found in the ECMM archive, if the archive has been correctly preserved, and they can be checked for correctness with the ECMM archive. I have been informed that a search has been made of the ECMM archive, and a great many reports with my name have been found, only a proportion of which were relevant to this trial. So it's possible that all of these reports that I found last night are already available and have been rejected as not relevant, but the Court may wish to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have no further questions, but we would ask the Court -- or we would like to make an application to at least be given the opportunity to review those additional 20 or so reports, including the report of September 4th, 1992, which I think was introduced as S215, which has the item of caveat and the language that was provided, although I appreciate Mr. Mayhew's recollection of that. We would like, if possible, to be able to examine the caveat that he placed and the reasons perhaps will enlighten us as to why objectivity and fairness to all sides was something that Mr. Mayhew, as he testified, was desirous of. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, there may be a problem over this. The documents, I think, are probably still the property of the European monitoring mission, or as it is now called the European Union Monitoring Mission. In order for anyone to have these documents, certainly the ones that we had in our possession, we had to get their permission to disclose, and I think we would need to make inquiries of that. The second thing about this is Mr. Mayhew is, in fact, due to return in September, if he still agrees after today, to testify in the Brdjanin/Talic case. So, it may be that we can deal with the authority that may be required. We haven't obviously -- because he was giving evidence, none of us could speak to him overnight none of us knew he had found these documents. But it seems to me rather than rush into this, we could see what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt that we have to be cautious on this issue, because even though the witness before us is or may be the author of these documents and the only author, he is not the owner of the documents. And therefore I would suggest the following: That the witness may give the diskette to the OTP. It's the witness of the OTP. And then the parties may, first of all, try to come to a conclusion amongst themselves how to proceed. No doubt, when it seems to be necessary to have the one or other document here present, then the authorisation of the owner of this document is required. As regards Document S215, to be honest, I can't see an obstacle to print out this document and substituting the word "caveat" what was deleted there, to bring it to our attention and distribute this page in the full version. Only as regards S215. And then please, the parties may confer about the future of all of the other documents contained in this diskette. Do you have the diskette with you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please hand it over after the hearing to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise for the lateness of discovery of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I'm acquainted with the rule that the witness, when appearing, is also preparing for the testimony himself in due time. But nevertheless, thank you for giving us this hint on this document, late but not too late.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's certainly not Mr. Mayhew's fault if anything because although we asked at the time, we didn't reask when we saw him yesterday. Your Honour, I do have one question in re-examination, if I may, before Your Honour questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: All the time you want until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Mayhew, of course, will be leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, proceed with the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one question, it was put to you that there was no such thing as a mayor in the Bosnian system. Can you tell us how you came to describe these persons that you saw such as Mr. Radic, the gentleman from Gradiska, as a mayor?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We also referred to Mr. Radic as the mayor of Banja Luka. So I am surprised to hear that in English translation, mayor is not a recognised term.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How did you come to understand the position that he held, which you equated with the English word "mayor"?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: We universally referred to Mr. Radic as the mayor of Banja Luka, and I'm certain that we would have been corrected many times by our interpreter if that was not the case, which leads me to the believe that the interpreter referred to him as the mayor in translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Two or three questions. On Exhibit Number S215, page 2, we can read at the end of paragraph 5: "The houses were burned" and then in parenthesis, to continue, "the team visited a part of Kozarac and found nearly all the houses burned. These houses were last seen by the ECMM in April intact and inhabited." Did you yourself see the houses burned?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw houses burned along that route. As I mentioned yesterday, I cannot with certainty remember whether I was part of the team going into Kozarac. I would have seen the edge of Kozarac from the road, houses in that area. But -- so I don't know whether I went into the part of Kozarac referred to here. It might have been a colleague of mine or myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you signed this report.

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you don't have your own knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was writing the report on behalf of the whole ECMM team that went that day. What I cannot recollect is the exact formation, makeup, of that team. If it was more than two people, it might have been other people within that team, and I'm signing this report on behalf of the whole team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see these houses as it's mentioned here Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in April "intact and inhabited?"

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, on that main route, and visiting those -- and visiting in the area, we saw all the houses along that route intact and inhabited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, just for clarification, you were already asked yesterday, and I apologise for the parties that I myself request quote only now by the concrete hour because it's not paginated what I have before me, it was at 15.26 yesterday. The question was: "Have you ever met Mr. Stakic on your earlier visits to Prijedor?" And then you said: "I don't know. I had certainly met the leader of the Serb community or Serb party in, as I mentioned earlier, but I don't remember his name." Then the question was do you think you would be able to recognise Dr. Stakic again? And then I was to a certain extent surprised, experienced with ordinary witness reaction. You even didn't look around in this courtroom. Have you seen in this courtroom any person, at least that you tried to find out where in this courtroom could a person that might be Dr. Stakic, why this reaction? Why didn't you try to find out?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the accused is sitting right there. I confined myself to answering the question strictly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I take it that you are not able to recognise Dr. Stakic at all?

utterances.speaker: JAMES BARNABAS BURKE MAYHEW [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not made it my business to look carefully at him, and so I haven't tried to recognise him. And the main reason for that is that I am not certain that I would be able to tell whether I recognised him or not. And I think it unlikely to be a reliable guide to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the basis of the answers provided yesterday and today, I don't want to go in any further details. Any questions from Judge Fassi Fihri? Judge Vassylenko? There are no further questions. The Defence, do you have any further questions emanating from my questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, I do have the time that the Court noted, 15.26.55, and that would be on page 29, lines 8 through 14 of that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance. If the witness would be then please so kind after having left the courtroom giving the diskette to a representative of the Prosecutor -- Office of the Prosecutor, you're excused. And thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Mayhew leaves, an investigator whom he has met is on her way down and will speak to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I have to inform the parties that during the last break, I got a letter of Madam Caillou telling me that she has made all necessary efforts that the expected witness for Monday will arrive on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, may I now that Mr. Mayhew has left, and I do very reluctantly. Your Honour, Mr. Mayhew, as with Mr. McLeod, came specially, cancelled a business engagement, to come to the Court. He's not, if I may say so, respectfully, like ordinary, everyday witnesses. And one of the things that Your Honour should know in particular in the light of Your Honour's last remark is that Mr. Mayhew comes from an English legal family, quite a well known one, and in England it is the law, and he knows it, that you can't make dock identifications. And that's why when -- I knew, because I asked him in advance whether he would recognise him, and he said no. And that's why I simply asked the question, so Your Honours would be aware that he couldn't recognise Dr. Stakic. Your Honours, I'm a little troubled, and I say so deeply respectfully about the attitude that Your Honour took to Mr. Mayhew. For the most part, it's not my job to protect witnesses. They come here, and they know what they are in for. But for the most part, Mr. Mayhew was doing his best to answer questions from either me or Mr. Ostojic, questions which Your Honours may have thought were badly phrased or went into details that were unnecessary. But it wasn't the witness's fault. And Your Honour, I am, as I say, and I do say so, with some reluctance, a little troubled about the manner that Your Honour adopted towards Mr. Mayhew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope it was clear enough that on this occasion, I didn't criticise either party. But nevertheless, on the basis of experience, having heard witnesses, asked witnesses myself, not only in my own legal system, admittedly it is very limited that I ever have seen a witness giving such statements which could lead to a misinterpretation of the answers. And I regard it as necessary that a witness tries to evade, to speculations, that I have to caution him. And I will do so also in the future because what we need here is facts, and sometimes, if, especially an inexperienced witness, answers a question where he cannot find any kind of basis for his answers, and to be very concrete, for the limited time he has been in the area and in Trnopolje, I regard it as my duty to caution the witness in the appropriate way. Nothing further should be said in this context, save that here, it was nothing in the direction of one or other party. The same was true already yesterday, and with a deep concern we saw the transcript of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On that note, Your Honour, I'm not going back to what I've raised, but as I said, Your Honour, it assists us if Your Honours make your concerns known, because as far as we're concerned, using the same word, the evidence that he gave was relevant and admissible, in particular, in respect of the visit to the camps that he went with. So if Your Honours are troubled, as I say, it helps if Your Honours indicate that either at the time or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But once again, to be extremely concrete, one reason for the problems arising here is that the Judges are not informed. We have to act on an uninformed basis. What we had before us, deciding whether or not we should hear the witness as a live witness, and not only to admit this document which could easily be introduced on the basis of the witness statement of Mr. McLeod, we were informed by the OTP that he met with Dr. Stakic in Prijedor who stated that Muslims were detained for their own safety. And as I said before, the OTP provides very, very limited evidence directly related to Dr. Stakic when it comes to witness evidence. And therefore, we have to rely on that information we get from the OTP. On this case, I have to re-emphasise the information we got was really misleading. We didn't have any additional material.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought Your Honours were supplied in advance with the statements and a list -- and the documents and a list that we were going to put in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We received this latter part one day before starting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand that. I appreciate that the Rule 65 ter summaries are in many cases very terse. But if Your Honours had felt, having seen, as I know Your Honours do, read the statement, that the evidence he was going to give was irrelevant, although as we say, we would submit it's highly relevant, then we would be grateful in future if Your Honours would indicate that to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On what basis, and when should we do so? And I have never said that the evidence given was irrelevant. Of course, as we said also in response to the motion of the Defence as regards another witness, it's later for the Judges to evaluate the probative value of a witness statement. And of course, we have to refrain from discussing these issues here and now. The only point is the parties are requesting us, and the rules are asking, that we are preparing our decisions, whether or not we introduce a witness statement under Rule 92 bis, and we can only do this when informed. And when we have this limited information of two lines and one word, and these two lines and one word are already this limited, information is misleading, then it is difficult to exercise conscientiously, our mandate. And as we did earlier, we would be more than eager to know the relevant information provided to the parties in advance that we can, on an adequate basis, decide whether or not to apply Rule 92 bis or not. And this was in this case the problem. And I think as regards the testimony as such, it was discussed enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I just then say, though, if Your Honours are going -- Your Honour is going to make a statement like "the transcript troubled you," we would wish to know because obviously, if it's a matter that Your Honours are going to take into consideration in any sort of deliberation, then we would ask respectfully that we get a chance to address any concerns Your Honours may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get the point about "transcript troubled you." This was only the problem. I was grateful that we got the assistance by the Defence giving us the page and it was only the question of the pagination today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour said earlier when you read the transcript from last night of yesterday's proceedings I think Your Honour used the word, that -- I'd have to go back, and said you were troubled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I'm addressing at the moment, that aspect. If Your Honours are troubled by something, we would be grateful for an indication as to what it is, so we can address the matter either by way of submission or any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think I did it sufficiently as regards the two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. last witnesses, taking into account that Witness S took us four hours, 43 minutes instead of envisaged one and a half hour. The cross-examination took exactly 28 minutes. And what my point was there, that this witness indeed could have been heard in the examination-in-chief in one and a half hour. Shall I really re-emphasise that we are spending not our money, but the money of the international taxpayer and we have to take care how we are spending our time. The trial stands adjourned until next Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
